After more than two years at reddit, I have resigned today. My first day was April 1, 2013 (goorangered!), and every day since has been an adventure.

In my eight months as reddit's CEO, I've seen the good, the bad and the ugly on reddit. The good has been off-the-wall inspiring, and the ugly made me doubt humanity.

I just want to remind everyone that I am just another human; I have a family, and I have feelings. Everyone attacked on reddit is just another person like you and me. When people make something up to attack me or someone else, it spreads, and we eventually will see it. And we will feel bad, not just about what was said. Also because it undercuts the authenticity of reddit and shakes our faith in humanity.

What has far outshone the hate has been the positive on reddit. Thank you, kind strangers, for expressing your support. You gilded me 100 times. (For those of you who apologized for generating a wave of accusations that I gilded myself, please don't feel bad. You did a good thing.) And thank you for sending cute animal pics and encouraging me to "Stay safe!" when the site overheated with expressions of hate in various forms. There were some days when your PMs inspired me more than you can imagine.

Most touching were the stories from regular users. Some told of people they knew who had committed suicide for being transgender or exposed in revenge porn. Others shared their experiences of being harassed and expressed empathy and gratitude. More recently, several users apologized for trolling me and for not giving me the benefit of the doubt when the troll hivemind moved against me. Initially users said they were afraid to post supportive messages openly; recently they started fighting back against the trolls publicly on reddit with support, corrections and positive messages.

So why am I leaving? Ultimately, the board asked me to demonstrate higher user growth in the next six months than I believe I can deliver while maintaining reddit's core principles.

You will be in good hands -- our strong leadership team will now be led by u/spez, one of reddit's original co-founders. Like u/kn0thing, he's lived and breathed reddit since its inception and will work passionately to ensure reddit's success.

Thank you to all the users who shared your excitement about reddit and what we've done and for encouraging everyone to remember the human. And thank you for making my time here at reddit an amazing learning experience.

The collected human knowledge and experience summed up does not scratch the surface of the known world. So knowing this, wouldn't it be arrogant (and ignorant!) to write any possibility off?

Humans are nowhere near aware of our own environment, not to mention the countless smaller and larger environments within and outside of our little blue spec. We like to vomit our seemingly deep perspectives while not really quantifying how poor our perception really is. Everything that we understand, and so use to create our society is good enough to keep it shambling forward, but that is all it is really capable of at this point.

Everything that we understand requires our environment to adhere to rules and have mathematical constants that we can always rely on to ground us in our calculations. The speed of light is supposed to be one of those constants. But if you look at the speed of light in the past, it hasn't always been the same. Though it has been stationary now for some time, what does that tell you about the laws and languages that we use to interpret our environment? To me it looks like there is reason to suspect that we haven't figured out as much as we think we have. But I can't be sure, I'm no expert after all, but would you call todays scientists, physicists and mathematicians experts of our physical world with their limited perspectives? It's hard to call anyone an expert when we can't explain half of the things that happen on a daily basis...

The pursuit of understanding the laws of physics and the language of math has become dogmatic, and because of this so has our progression as a race. How can we presume that anything in our universe is fixed when we don't even know the extent of our environment? Or understand what consciousness is? Science isn't advanced enough for us to prove that god isn't real. We are still smashing large cubes into small circular holes here in the (seemingly) 3rd dimension, so where does this arrogance come from? If god is real it sure as hell isn't like humans have ever imagined it, and would probably just be apart of some different process of the universe that sometimes bears to existence... existence, consciousness! In reality god could just be a huge mass, ebbing and flowing like a tide, but to us it is god, as we are left in its' wake to squirm and claw our way through squalor and dying light.

All of our experience and knowledge doesn't belong to all of humanity, it exists in chunks here and there. Some of it hidden away, secret. The majority is spread over every individual. We as individuals cannot easily process each others experiences and knowledge. Our ways of communicating has improved over time, but we still can't truly process each others experiences and knowledge without painstaking measures and long deliberations and testing and... smashing cubes into circle shaped holes. Imagine if we were connected, and all we had to do to show someone what another saw, how they felt, where they are, or what they learned was to let them experience it themselves? What if these connections exist already and we don't have a way to utilize them? Perhaps this digital age is just a fancy analog and we haven't begun to understand what digital really is.

Sorry for the rant, thanks if you read it. My bad if you feel dumber after my what-if-alanche concussed you into a mental vegetation.

Tl;dr: Humans can't observe shit, so don't assume anything you've learned will always hold any actual meaning in reality. God could be real! Maybe our imagining god is what gave birth to god? Point being, we won't find out shit either way if our race doesn't stop pussy footing around with filling up metal cubes with money, and hoarding the entirety of a spec of resources that the earth has to offer, simply to hold dominion over ourselves, indefinitely.

I have all but stopped talking about what I consider irrational beliefs, unless I know that the person I'm speaking with is on the same page as me. If it comes up naturally and I'm asked where I stand on a subject (like religion), I will briefly state it and then drop it. I don't engage in debates anymore.

In my experience almost everyone has their blind spots. Some people have a lot, some have very few or just one blatant one, but everyone has them. That most likely includes me, but I couldn't begin to tell you where it is (obviously).

Irrational beliefs often have nothing to do with intelligence.

  • There are people like Francis Collins, a leader in the ambitious Human Genome Project, who are brilliant scientists, but also religious. Sure, they may be in the minority, but they exist.
  • I have a friend who is an atheist like me, has no patience for bullshit, but talks about astrological signs all the time. I don't bring it up.
  • I have another friend who is a psychologist in his early 60s and one of the wisest people I know. Considers astrology nothing more than "mathematical equations". Also thinks the internet is evil (he's not religious).
  • The best teacher I've ever had in my life (bar none) believes in pretty much everything irrational - Tarot, magical spells, conspiracy theories, astrology (while being a hobby astronomer), dowsing - you name it, he believes in it. He thinks religion is stupid. He is also one of the nicest, friendlist, loveliest people I've ever met (as long as we talk don't talk about his woo-woo). He teaches math btw and he's brilliant at it.

I found that pointing things out, even just asking questions that mildly imply that they might not be entirely right, hurts feelings. It's a damn shame and makes human interactions much harder for me.

I wonder if I have a blatant blind spot like that. It doesn't feel like I do, because I definitely feel like I'm trying to be as rational about things as I can possibly be. But I'm willing to bet that most people feel the same.

Anyway, I'd agree that what I consider rationality ultimately consists of beliefs as well. I don't spend hours a day reading scientific studies. In the end, you could say that I'm just putting my trust in different people (scientists) or a different system (science) than the aforementioned people do. I think it's a sensible thing to "believe in science" because the process has been proven to work for generations now, but in the end I don't know shit aside from the stuff I work with in my job (which has nothing to do with science).
